top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: A total of eight cross- sectional studies were included in the meta- analysis. We identified 3775 articles by searching the databases MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase (Ovid) and Web of Science. A total of 1456 studies were excluded because of duplication, while 1565 were classified as ineligible by automation tools. Another 546 studies were removed for additional reasons. We examined the titles and abstracts of 208 studies and excluded 157 on the basis of our findings. We screened 51 articles for eligibility. Eight studies were included in the meta- analysis. The PRISMA flow chart is shown in figure 1.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: The results of the individual studies are presented in figure 2. Children and adolescents with low adherence to the MedDiet had greater odds of developing MetS compared to those with medium to high adherence. The OR for this association was 2.18, with a 95% CI ranging from 1.45 to 3.28 ( p < 0.001). The inconsistency among the studies, as assessed by the I² statistic, was 64.15%.

top_evidence.text: The extracted data were systematised via a specially constructed standardised data extraction form (see study protocol), and the extracted data were then reviewed for consistency by the reviewers. Each included study was independently reviewed for critical appraisal and bias reduction, and a modified version of the Newcastle Ottawa cohort scale was used for cross- sectional research (online supplemental file 1). 29 Consensus was used to settle disagreements; the results are shown in table 1. Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta- analysis
top_evidence.text: The association between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents has been a topic of increasing interest in recent years. Our study revealed that children and adolescents with lower MedDiet adherence had a greater risk of MetS than did those with higher adherence, providing important insights into the potential benefits of the MedDiet for MetS in children and adolescents. Specifically, higher adherence to the MedDiet was associated with lower odds of MetS, which includes a clustering of metabolic abnormalities such as abdominal obesity, high blood pressure, dyslipidaemia and impaired glucose metabolism. top_evidence.text: Two authors independently conducted systematic searches in the following databases: Excerpta Medica Database (Embase, via OvidSP), Scopus, Web of Science and PubMed. The searches included studies published from database inception to 22 April 2024. The search was limited to peer- reviewed studies published in English. A professional librarian was consulted to ensure the quality of the search strategy.
